title: minute-token-amortization-cheatsheet
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad for thinking about minute-level (and per-session) token amortization — how to translate GPU / capacity / SLA costs into per-minute credits and microtier pricing. Not polished; testing assumptions and edge cases.

Key high-level idea:
- Move away from pure per-token pricing for micro-interactive flows where latency SLO + concurrency drive cost. Charge a small per-minute reserve (credits burned while session active) + per-token for heavy generative work. That stabilizes revenue and lets us underwrite low-latency reserved capacity for free-tier/pro TOT.

Assumptions (base case):
- GPU cost to us (amortized infra + ops) = $2.40 / GPU-hour (example after reserved discounts).
- Effective serving throughput (avg tokens/sec usable per GPU across mixed models) = 600 tokens/sec (batching + KV cache helps).
- So cost per token = ($2.40 / 3600s) / 600 tps = $0.00000111 per token ~ 1.1e-6 USD/token.
- But heavily latency-sensitive requests reduce batching -> effective tokens/sec drops to 150 tps -> cost/token ~ 4.4e-6 USD/token.

Why per-minute matters:
- Interactive UXs keep KV caches warm; small repeated calls have very low marginal token cost but occupy concurrency slots and KV cache that lower overall GPU efficiency.
- If a user opens a session and makes 1 request every 30s (low token volume), they still block an instance of the runtime. Without a time-based charge we subsidize that idle tail.

Minute-amortization model (sketch):
- Reserve-credit burn = X credits / active-minute. Define 1 credit ~= $0.0005 (configurable).
- For baseline microtier target: want to recover 20% of effective GPU-minute cost per active slot from reserve charge (rest from per-token / other uses).
- If low-latency slot cost per minute (accounting infra + SRE) = $0.04 / minute (example: $2.40 / hour), 20% = $0.008/minute -> X credits = $0.008 / 0.0005 = 16 credits/min.
- So rough: charge 16 credits/min while session active, plus per-token at a small multiplier to cover heavy tokens.

Token math examples (3 scenarios):
1) Latency-sensitive chat (many short prompts):
   - Session: 10 minutes, 12 prompts, avg 80 tokens each => total tokens 960.
   - Reserve burn: 10 * 16 = 160 credits.
   - Token burn: 960 tokens * 1 credit/1000 tokens (placeholder) = 0.96 credits.
   - Total ~161 credits => mostly from minute charge.

2) Bulk generation (background batch):
   - Session: 5 minutes active, single call emits 50k tokens.
   - Reserve burn: 5 * 16 = 80 credits.
   - Token burn: 50,000 * (1 credit / 1000 tokens) = 50 credits.
   - Total 130 credits -> token cost more significant here.

3) Idle open tab (keeps socket/polling):
   - Session: 60 min, 0 tokens after initial warm-up.
   - Reserve burn: 60 * 16 = 960 credits => we need a cap/decay to avoid abuse.

Design knobs / mitigations:
- Idle grace window: first N minutes free per session (e.g., 2 minutes) to cover short interactions.
- Exponential decay: after 10 minutes of inactivity, burn rate drops to 25% (keeps KV but lowers cost).
- Max daily/reserve cap per user to avoid runaway charges.
- Different reserve rates per plan: free/dev = 8 credits/min (we subsidize more), pro = 32 credits/min (we guarantee lower latency), enterprise = negotiated.
- Burst credits: provide monthly burst pool for free users (e.g., 10k credits) to encourage discovery.

Back-of-envelope unit economics mapping: credits -> USD -> GPU minutes
- If 1 credit = $0.0005, then 120 credits = $0.06 -> buys 1.5 minutes of GPU (based on $0.04/min). So 1 minute reserve (16 credits) equals $0.008 cost to us. 
- If average micro-user session = 7 minutes/day -> daily reserve burn = 112 credits -> monthly ~3.36k credits -> $1.68 / user / month just in reserve burn. Useful when projecting CAC payback.

Tier ideas (brief prototypes):
- Free tier: 0 credits/min first 2 minutes, then 8 credits/min; 3k monthly free credits; per-token rate higher. Encourages short experimentation.
- Developer: 8 credits/min baseline, low token price, monthly commit discount.
- Pro: 16-24 credits/min, lower per-token price, higher concurrency, lower latency SLO.
- Teams/Enterprise: custom reserve rates, pool sharing, SLA-backed slot guarantees, commitment discounts.

Edge-cases & abuse vectors:
- Background polling: clients can send tiny pings to maintain session. Need heartbeat validation (only count if websocket active + recent real requests) or require keepalive ping cost > 0 tokens or enforce inactivity decay.
- Long idle tabs for bots: per-user caps and heuristics (max active-minutes per day before manual review).

Quick heuristics to test in simulations:
1) Vary avg tokens/sec from 150 -> 1200 and compute break-even per-minute charge to maintain 20% margin.
2) Simulate 100k daily users with mix: 70% short chat, 20% bulk, 10% idle -> compute expected credits/month and revenue.
3) Run CAC payback sensitivity: if average ARPU after reserve = $3/month, what CAC is acceptable for self-serve?

Unresolved questions (TODO):
- Exact credit <-> USD mapping: keep it simple but avoid too many decimals. 
- UX: how to show reserve burn live in console without confusing users.
- Integrations: how does reserve interact with Dedicated capacity billing? (Probably offset by committed pool).
- Legal/regulatory: disclosures for automatic reserve drain and refunds.

Notes to self / action items:
- Build small sim (notebook) to sweep reserve_rate, idle_decay, user segments and output monthly revenue + 95th percentile per-user spend. (JIRA PRIC-478)
- Prototype a UI tooltip: “Reserve credits keep your session warm; you can close the session to stop burning.”
- Ask SRE: realistic per-slot cost for low-latency pinned instances (include SLO ops overhead).

Slack refs / possible copy snippets:
- quick channel ping: "pricing: trying minute-burn model to stabilize micro-interactive economics — ping if you have catastro cases"

Random heuristics I liked in tests:
- If reserve_rate == 1 credit/min and 1 credit == $0.001, people feel the charge is negligible for short flows but it scales for long tail -> good for discovery.
- Tiering the reserve (not just token) gives us a simple dial for SLA: higher reserve -> more capacity priority.

End of scratchpad.

Questions I still have (for next session):
- Do we want reserve charges to be mandatory for sockets or opt-in as a paid enhancement?
- How would this interact with concurrency-limited API keys vs session-based keys?
